items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “a critical survey of existing research on a question, identifying debates, findings and gaps”?
items.answer: Literature review
items.markingKey: Literature review: a critical survey of existing research on a question, identifying debates, findings and gaps. [1]

items.stem: Tanaka (2013), studying West Africa, found mixed results, depending on how strongly governments enforced the policy; Moreau (2023), studying North America, found evidence supporting the view that votes at 16 could build a habit of lifelong participation. Which sentence best synthesises these studies in a literature review on lowering the voting age to 16?
options: Both studies prove that the voting age should be lowered to 16.
Tanaka (2013) and Moreau (2023) reach different conclusions, possibly because they studied different regions (West Africa and North America).
Tanaka (2013) studied West Africa. Moreau (2023) studied North America.
Moreau (2023) is more recent, so Tanaka (2013) can be ignored.
items.answer: Tanaka (2013) and Moreau (2023) reach different conclusions, possibly because they studied different regions (West Africa and North America).
items.markingKey: Synthesis compares and explains the relationship between findings rather than listing or dismissing them. [1]

items.stem: Silva (2016), studying North America, found evidence supporting the view that compulsory voting would make elected governments more representative; Moreau (2019), studying the Middle East, found evidence supporting the opposing view that compulsory voting removes the freedom not to vote. Which sentence best synthesises these studies in a literature review on low voter turnout among young people?
options: Silva (2016) and Moreau (2019) reach different conclusions, possibly because they studied different regions (North America and the Middle East).
Silva (2016) studied North America. Moreau (2019) studied the Middle East.
Both studies prove that voting should be made compulsory.
Moreau (2019) is more recent, so Silva (2016) can be ignored.
items.answer: Silva (2016) and Moreau (2019) reach different conclusions, possibly because they studied different regions (North America and the Middle East).
items.markingKey: Synthesis compares and explains the relationship between findings rather than listing or dismissing them. [1]

items.stem: A student researching “How far do the benefits outweigh the drawbacks of the proposal that the dam operator should share real-time data on dam filling and river flows?” has read three studies. Kowalski (2016) studied Latin America and found evidence supporting the view that shared rules can make water a source of cooperation rather than conflict. Nguyen (2017) studied East Africa and found evidence supporting the opposing view that upstream countries have the right to use resources on their own territory. Mensah (2018) studied South-East Asia and found mixed results, depending on how strongly governments enforced the policy. Write a sentence that synthesises two of the studies.
items.answer: e.g. “While Kowalski (2016) found evidence supporting the view that shared rules can make water a source of cooperation rather than conflict, Nguyen (2017) found evidence supporting the opposing view that upstream countries have the right to use resources on their own territory, suggesting that context shapes the outcome.”
items.markingKey: 1 mark compares; 1 mark explains relationship [2]

items.stem: A student researching “Should governments be allowed to use live facial recognition in public places?” has read three studies. Tanaka (2017) studied South-East Asia and found evidence supporting the view that the technology threatens the rights of innocent people. Silva (2018) studied the Middle East and found mixed results, depending on how strongly governments enforced the policy. Kowalski (2023) studied East Africa and found evidence supporting the opposing view that the technology helps police find missing people and dangerous suspects. (a) Identify a possible research gap. (b) Explain one limitation of relying on Tanaka (2017).
items.answer: (a) e.g. none of the studies examines the student’s own region, or recent years, or the perspective of the people most affected. (b) It is the oldest study (2017); circumstances, laws or technology may have changed since, so its findings may be out of date.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark [1] (b) 1 mark currency; 1 mark applied [2]

items.stem: A student researching “To what extent is it the responsibility of the exporting governments to address state use of facial recognition surveillance?” has read three studies. Haddad (2016) studied the Middle East and found mixed results, depending on how strongly governments enforced the policy. Ramírez (2020) studied Latin America and found evidence supporting the view that the technology threatens the rights of innocent people. Banerjee (2023) studied South Asia and found evidence supporting the opposing view that the technology helps police find missing people and dangerous suspects. (a) Suggest one reason why the studies reached different conclusions. (b) Write a sentence that synthesises two of the studies.
items.answer: (a) Different regions and political contexts, different time periods, or different methods and definitions. (b) e.g. “While Haddad (2016) found mixed results, depending on how strongly governments enforced the policy, Ramírez (2020) found evidence supporting the view that the technology threatens the rights of innocent people, suggesting that context shapes the outcome.”
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark reason; 1 mark linked to the studies [2] (b) 1 mark compares; 1 mark explains relationship [2]

items.stem: “Grey literature from NGOs and governments is as valuable as academic research for a report on low voter turnout among young people.” Discuss this claim, considering arguments for and against before reaching a supported conclusion.
items.answer: For: NGO and government reports are often more current and contain field data. They reveal the perspectives of key stakeholders. Against: They are not peer reviewed and may reflect vested interests. Academic research uses transparent methods and engages with theory. Judgement: Grey literature is valuable for perspectives and recent data, but must be evaluated and corroborated against academic research.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.answer: Primary research
items.markingKey: Primary research: collecting new data directly, for example through surveys, interviews or experiments. [1]

items.stem: Explain what is wrong with this survey question and rewrite it: “Should our weak and useless leaders finally do something about state use of facial recognition surveillance?”
items.answer: Loaded wording: emotive words push respondents towards one answer. Improved, e.g.: “To what extent do you agree or disagree that governments should ban live facial recognition in public places? (Strongly agree / Agree / Neither / Disagree / Strongly disagree)”.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies fault; 1 mark explains effect on data; 1 mark neutral, single, clear rewrite [3]

items.stem: Explain what is wrong with this survey question and rewrite it: “Do you think the export of plastic waste to poorer countries is serious and that the parties to the Basel Convention should tighten international rules on plastic waste trade?”
items.answer: Double-barrelled question: it asks two things at once, so one answer cannot be interpreted. Improved, e.g.: “To what extent do you agree or disagree that richer countries should be banned from exporting plastic waste? (Strongly agree / Agree / Neither / Disagree / Strongly disagree)”.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies fault; 1 mark explains effect on data; 1 mark neutral, single, clear rewrite [3]

items.stem: Sofia is researching “To what extent is it the responsibility of the governments and civil society groups to address the spread of online disinformation during elections?”. The plan is to hand out a questionnaire to friends in the school canteen, including the question “Should our weak and useless leaders finally do something about the spread of online disinformation during elections?”, and to interview one local politician. Identify the sampling method and one weakness.
items.answer: Opportunity sampling: friends in the canteen are unlikely to represent all students.
items.markingKey: 1 mark method; 1 mark weakness [2]

items.stem: Hana is researching “Should richer countries be banned from exporting plastic waste?”. The plan is to hand out a questionnaire to friends in the school canteen, including the question “Do you often think about the export of plastic waste to poorer countries?”, and to interview one local politician. (a) Explain the problem with the survey question. (b) Suggest one advantage of the interview.
items.answer: (a) Ambiguous question: “often” means different things to different respondents. (b) It provides in-depth, qualitative insight into an expert/stakeholder perspective that a questionnaire cannot.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark fault; 1 mark effect on data [2] (b) 1 mark [1]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that interviews are more useful than questionnaires for researching perspectives on the under-representation of women in parliaments.
items.answer: For: Interviews reveal reasons and values behind a perspective. Follow-up questions clarify meaning. Against: Questionnaires reach larger, more representative samples. Closed questions produce data that can be compared and analysed statistically. Judgement: The best choice depends on the question; many reports combine both (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.stem: Explain what is wrong with this survey question and rewrite it: “Do you often think about disputes over shared rivers?”
items.answer: Ambiguous question: “often” means different things to different respondents. Improved, e.g.: “To what extent do you agree or disagree that upstream countries should agree dam operations with downstream neighbours? (Strongly agree / Agree / Neither / Disagree / Strongly disagree)”.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies fault; 1 mark explains effect on data; 1 mark neutral, single, clear rewrite [3]

items.stem: Kenji is researching “To what extent is reform of the UN Security Council best addressed through national rather than international action?”. The plan is to hand out a questionnaire to friends in the school canteen, including the question “Do you think reform of the UN Security Council is serious and that the UN member states should abolish or restrict the veto for cases of mass atrocities?”, and to interview one local politician. Identify the sampling method and one weakness.
items.answer: Opportunity sampling: friends in the canteen are unlikely to represent all students.
items.markingKey: 1 mark method; 1 mark weakness [2]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “the consistency of a method: whether it would give similar results if repeated”?
items.answer: Reliability
items.markingKey: Reliability: the consistency of a method: whether it would give similar results if repeated. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): A method can be reliable without being valid. Reason (R): A survey can give consistent results while measuring the wrong thing. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: Both true; R explains A. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): Triangulation strengthens research findings. Reason (R): If different methods give the same result, the finding is less likely to be an artefact of one method. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: Both true; R explains A. [1]

items.stem: A survey of 625 randomly selected adults finds 55% support for the proposal that the parties to the Basel Convention should tighten international rules on plastic waste trade. The approximate 95% margin of error is given by 1/√n × 100 percentage points. What is the margin of error?
items.answer: ±4 percentage points

items.stem: A survey of 400 randomly selected adults finds 54% support for the proposal that the parliament should protect journalists’ sources and repeal broad “false news” laws. The approximate 95% margin of error is given by 1/√n × 100 percentage points. Calculate the margin of error and the likely range of true support. Can the researcher conclude that a majority supports the proposal?
items.answer: 1/√400 × 100 = ±5 points; range 49% to 59%. The range includes 50% or less, so a majority cannot be concluded.
items.markingKey: 1 mark margin; 1 mark range; 1 mark correct conclusion [3]

items.stem: A survey of 2,500 randomly selected adults finds 53% support for the proposal that the parliament should protect journalists’ sources and repeal broad “false news” laws. The approximate 95% margin of error is given by 1/√n × 100 percentage points. Calculate the margin of error and the likely range of true support. Can the researcher conclude that a majority supports the proposal? Explain why the margin of error does not account for all sources of error.
items.answer: 1/√2,500 × 100 = ±2 points; range 51% to 55%. The whole range is above 50%, so a majority is likely. It covers random sampling error only, not bias from question wording, non-response or a non-random sample.
items.markingKey: 1 mark margin; 1 mark range; 1 mark correct conclusion; 1 mark only random error; 1 mark example of systematic bias [5]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that student primary research adds little of value to a report on reform of the UN Security Council compared with published research.
items.answer: For: Student samples are small and unrepresentative. Published research uses larger samples and peer-reviewed methods. Against: Primary research can explore a local context or perspective that published research ignores. Triangulating local data with published studies can reveal differences. Judgement: Primary research is most valuable when clearly limited in its claims and used alongside published evidence.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.stem: A student uses a peer-reviewed article in an academic political science journal as evidence in a report on lowering the voting age to 16. Evaluate its credibility.
items.answer: Strength: other experts checked its methods before publication. Weakness: it may be several years old or focus on a narrow case. It should be corroborated by independent evidence.
items.markingKey: 1 mark strength; 1 mark weakness; 1 mark corroboration or judgement [3]

items.stem: Assertion (A): A large sample always guarantees generalisable results. Reason (R): Biased sampling methods can produce unrepresentative samples of any size. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: A is false, but R is true.
items.markingKey: A false; R true. [1]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “numerical data that can be counted or measured”?
items.answer: Quantitative data
items.markingKey: Quantitative data: numerical data that can be counted or measured. [1]

items.stem: A report on migration caused by climate change includes evidence from UNHCR (recognises climate change as a driver of displacement but uses the existing definition of a refugee) and from the government of a low-lying Pacific island state (demands that high-emitting countries accept responsibility). Explain how the student could synthesise these perspectives rather than simply describe them.
items.answer: Identify where they agree and disagree, explain why (e.g. it must work within the mandate states have given it; its territory may become uninhabitable), weigh the quality of the evidence each uses, and combine insights into a judgement on the question.
items.markingKey: 1 mark agreement/disagreement; 1 mark explains differences; 1 mark weighs evidence; 1 mark combined judgement [4]

items.stem: A report on the spread of online disinformation during elections includes evidence from a social media company (prefers voluntary codes of conduct to new laws) and from a press freedom organisation (warns against laws that let governments define “fake news”). Explain how the student could synthesise these perspectives rather than simply describe them.
items.answer: Identify where they agree and disagree, explain why (e.g. regulation would raise its costs and legal risks; such laws have been used to jail journalists), weigh the quality of the evidence each uses, and combine insights into a judgement on the question.
items.markingKey: 1 mark agreement/disagreement; 1 mark explains differences; 1 mark weighs evidence; 1 mark combined judgement [4]

items.stem: Respondents rated the statement “Social media companies should be legally responsible for false political content” on a 1–5 scale. Responses: 1 Strongly disagree: 2; 2 Disagree: 2; 3 Neutral: 4; 4 Agree: 5; 5 Strongly agree: 8. What is the modal response?
items.answer: 5 Strongly agree
items.markingKey: Most frequent = 5 Strongly agree (8). [1]

items.stem: Survey results on whether the parliament should introduce legal candidate quotas requiring parties to field a minimum share of women: Group | Support | Total asked. Under 25 | 57 | 80. 25 and over | 85 | 200. Calculate the percentage support in each group and overall. Explain why comparing the raw numbers who support the proposal would be misleading.
items.answer: Under 25: 57/80 = 71.2%; 25 and over: 85/200 = 42.5%; overall 142/280 = 50.7%. Groups are different sizes, so raw counts (57 vs 85) do not show relative support; percentages do.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each group %; 1 mark overall %; 1 mark explains different group sizes [4]

items.stem: A student researching “Should the permanent members of the UN Security Council lose their veto power?” has three kinds of evidence: a survey of 300 adults (58% support the proposal that the UN member states should abolish or restrict the veto for cases of mass atrocities); 12 interviews, mostly expressing the concern that the permanent members would have to agree, and they can veto Charter amendments; and a peer-reviewed study finding that the veto prevents the Council from fulfilling its responsibility for international peace. (a) Explain why the survey and interviews appear to disagree. (b) Explain how qualitative evidence adds to the quantitative evidence.
items.answer: (a) The survey measures overall support; interviewees, a smaller and possibly unrepresentative group, explain concerns. Support and concern can coexist. (b) It explains reasons and values behind the numbers, revealing concerns that a percentage hides.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark different measures; 1 mark sample difference [2] (b) 1 mark reasons; 1 mark example [2]

items.stem: Respondents rated the statement “Upstream countries should agree dam operations with downstream neighbours” on a 1–5 scale. Responses: 1 Strongly disagree: 19; 2 Disagree: 20; 3 Neutral: 7; 4 Agree: 14; 5 Strongly agree: 3. What is the modal response?
items.answer: 2 Disagree
items.markingKey: Most frequent = 2 Disagree (20). [1]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “evaluation of a study by independent experts before publication”?
items.answer: Peer review
items.markingKey: Peer review: evaluation of a study by independent experts before publication. [1]

items.stem: Banerjee (2014), studying North America, found evidence supporting the opposing view that sanctions helped end apartheid in South Africa; Kowalski (2018), studying Latin America, found mixed results, depending on how strongly governments enforced the policy. Which sentence best synthesises these studies in a literature review on the use of economic sanctions?
options: Both studies prove that economic sanctions are rarely an effective way to change a government’s behaviour.
Banerjee (2014) and Kowalski (2018) reach different conclusions, possibly because they studied different regions (North America and Latin America).
Banerjee (2014) studied North America. Kowalski (2018) studied Latin America.
Kowalski (2018) is more recent, so Banerjee (2014) can be ignored.
items.answer: Banerjee (2014) and Kowalski (2018) reach different conclusions, possibly because they studied different regions (North America and Latin America).
items.markingKey: Synthesis compares and explains the relationship between findings rather than listing or dismissing them. [1]

items.stem: Explain two purposes of a literature review in a research report on disputes over shared rivers.
items.answer: It places the question in its academic context and identifies the main debates and perspectives; it reveals gaps that the report can address; synthesis shows how findings relate, rather than listing them.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each purpose, 1 mark each developed [4]

items.stem: A student researching “To what extent is the under-representation of women in parliaments best addressed through national rather than international action?” has read three studies. Okafor (2013) studied North America and found evidence supporting the view that legal requirements are needed to change who is selected. Tanaka (2015) studied Latin America and found mixed results, depending on how strongly governments enforced the policy. Novak (2017) studied Western Europe and found evidence supporting the opposing view that quotas mean candidates are chosen because of gender rather than ability. Write a sentence that synthesises two of the studies.
items.answer: e.g. “While Okafor (2013) found evidence supporting the view that legal requirements are needed to change who is selected, Tanaka (2015) found mixed results, depending on how strongly governments enforced the policy, suggesting that context shapes the outcome.”
items.markingKey: 1 mark compares; 1 mark explains relationship [2]

items.stem: A student’s reading list on lowering the voting age to 16 has 32 sources: 15 peer-reviewed articles, 7 reports by governments and NGOs, and 10 news or opinion pieces. 6 of the peer-reviewed articles were published more than ten years ago. Calculate the percentage of sources that are peer-reviewed, and the percentage of the peer-reviewed articles that are more than ten years old. Comment on the balance of the reading list.
items.answer: 15/32 × 100 = 46.9% peer-reviewed; 6/15 × 100 = 40% of these are over ten years old. Under half the list is academic, so the student should add more peer-reviewed research, and recent studies are needed to keep the review current; news pieces are useful for perspectives but weaker as evidence.
items.markingKey: 1 mark peer-reviewed %; 1 mark old %; 1 mark comment on academic balance; 1 mark comment on currency [4]

items.answer: Closed question

items.stem: Mohammed is researching “How far do the benefits outweigh the drawbacks of the proposal that the national government should publish all public contracts online (open contracting)?”. The plan is to hand out a questionnaire to friends in the school canteen, including the question “Do you think corruption in public procurement is serious and that the national government should publish all public contracts online (open contracting)?”, and to interview one local politician. Explain one limitation of interviewing only one politician.
items.answer: One person represents only one perspective and may have a vested interest; findings cannot be generalised.
items.markingKey: 1 mark one perspective/bias; 1 mark generalisation [2]

items.stem: What is meant by “reliability” in Global Perspectives?
options: The percentage of people asked to take part who actually respond.
The tendency of respondents to give answers that make them look good.
Using more than one method or source to check findings.
The consistency of a method: whether it would give similar results if repeated.
items.answer: The consistency of a method: whether it would give similar results if repeated.
items.markingKey: Reliability: the consistency of a method: whether it would give similar results if repeated. [1]

items.stem: A student uses a leaflet produced by a political party during an election campaign as evidence in a report on the under-representation of women in parliaments. Evaluate its credibility.
items.answer: Strength: it states the party’s position clearly. Weakness: its purpose is to win votes, so it is likely to be one-sided. It should be corroborated by independent evidence.
items.markingKey: 1 mark strength; 1 mark weakness; 1 mark corroboration or judgement [3]

items.stem: A student emails a questionnaire about corruption in public procurement to 250 people and receives 69 replies. What is the response rate?

A student researching the under-representation of women in parliaments surveyed 60 classmates (opportunity sample) using Likert-scale questions, and interviewed one official from UN Women. The student concludes that “people in our country support the view that countries should introduce legal gender quotas for parliament”. Explain why the conclusion cannot be generalised.
items.answer: 60 classmates from one school are not representative of the national population (age, location, background).
items.markingKey: 1 mark small/unrepresentative; 1 mark linked to “people in our country” [2]

items.stem: A student emails a questionnaire about migration caused by climate change to 400 people and receives 112 replies. Calculate the response rate and explain how non-response could affect the validity of the findings.
items.answer: 112/400 × 100 = 28%. People who reply may differ from those who do not (e.g. more interested or with stronger views), so results may not represent the whole group.
items.markingKey: 1 mark response rate; 1 mark non-respondents may differ; 1 mark effect on validity/generalisation [3]

items.answer: Identify where they agree and disagree, explain why (e.g. she has personal experience of the selection process; it works for gender equality under SDG 5), weigh the quality of the evidence each uses, and combine insights into a judgement on the question.

items.stem: A report on corruption in public procurement includes evidence from Transparency International (campaigns for open contracting and stronger enforcement) and from a business association (supports simpler procurement rules). Explain how the student could synthesise these perspectives rather than simply describe them.
items.answer: Identify where they agree and disagree, explain why (e.g. it is an NGO whose mission is to fight corruption; complex rules raise costs for its members), weigh the quality of the evidence each uses, and combine insights into a judgement on the question.
items.markingKey: 1 mark agreement/disagreement; 1 mark explains differences; 1 mark weighs evidence; 1 mark combined judgement [4]

items.stem: Survey results on whether the United Nations member states should extend refugee protection to people displaced by climate change: Group | Support | Total asked. Under 25 | 61 | 150. 25 and over | 101 | 200. What percentage of the Under 25 group supports the proposal?

“Quantitative data are more persuasive than qualitative data in a report on migration caused by climate change.” Discuss this claim, considering arguments for and against before reaching a supported conclusion.
items.answer: For: Numbers summarise large samples and can be compared. Statistics appear objective to readers. Against: Qualitative data explain the reasons behind perspectives. Numbers can mislead through sampling or presentation. Judgement: Persuasiveness depends on quality and fit to the question; synthesis of both is strongest.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “an aspect of a question that existing research has not yet answered”?
items.answer: Research gap
items.markingKey: Research gap: an aspect of a question that existing research has not yet answered. [1]

items.stem: Nguyen (2014), studying East Africa, found evidence supporting the view that open contracting makes corruption harder to hide; Adeyemi (2022), studying West Africa, found mixed results, depending on how strongly governments enforced the policy. Which sentence best synthesises these studies in a literature review on corruption in public procurement?
options: Both studies prove that every government should publish all public contracts online.
Nguyen (2014) and Adeyemi (2022) reach different conclusions, possibly because they studied different regions (East Africa and West Africa).
Adeyemi (2022) is more recent, so Nguyen (2014) can be ignored.
Nguyen (2014) studied East Africa. Adeyemi (2022) studied West Africa.
items.answer: Nguyen (2014) and Adeyemi (2022) reach different conclusions, possibly because they studied different regions (East Africa and West Africa).
items.markingKey: Synthesis compares and explains the relationship between findings rather than listing or dismissing them. [1]

items.stem: Explain why a literature review should do more than summarise sources one by one.
items.answer: It places the question in its academic context and identifies the main debates and perspectives; it reveals gaps that the report can address; synthesis shows how findings relate, rather than listing them.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each purpose, 1 mark each developed [4]

items.stem: A student researching “Are economic sanctions an effective way to change a government’s behaviour?” has read three studies. Petrov (2012) studied South-East Asia and found evidence supporting the view that sanctions often strengthen rather than weaken the targeted regime. Tanaka (2014) studied West Africa and found mixed results, depending on how strongly governments enforced the policy. Banerjee (2015) studied Latin America and found evidence supporting the opposing view that sanctions helped end apartheid in South Africa. Explain one limitation of relying on Petrov (2012).
items.answer: It is the oldest study (2012); circumstances, laws or technology may have changed since, so its findings may be out of date.
items.markingKey: 1 mark currency; 1 mark applied [2]

items.stem: A student researching “How far do the benefits outweigh the drawbacks of the proposal that the exporting governments should ban exports and build domestic recycling capacity?” has read three studies. Haddad (2017) studied South Asia and found mixed results, depending on how strongly governments enforced the policy. Silva (2020) studied the Middle East and found evidence supporting the opposing view that trade in sorted, clean plastic provides useful raw materials. Kowalski (2022) studied South-East Asia and found evidence supporting the view that exporting waste shifts the harm onto poorer communities. (a) Identify one point of disagreement between the studies. (b) Explain one limitation of relying on Haddad (2017).
items.answer: (a) Haddad found mixed results, depending on how strongly governments enforced the policy, whereas Silva found evidence supporting the opposing view that trade in sorted, clean plastic provides useful raw materials. (b) It is the oldest study (2017); circumstances, laws or technology may have changed since, so its findings may be out of date.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark identifies; 1 mark supported with authors [2] (b) 1 mark currency; 1 mark applied [2]

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that grey literature from NGOs and governments is as valuable as academic research for a report on disputes over shared rivers? Consider different perspectives in your answer.
items.answer: For: NGO and government reports are often more current and contain field data. They reveal the perspectives of key stakeholders. Against: They are not peer reviewed and may reflect vested interests. Academic research uses transparent methods and engages with theory. Judgement: Grey literature is valuable for perspectives and recent data, but must be evaluated and corroborated against academic research.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–5 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (6–8 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [8]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “a question that lets respondents answer in their own words, producing qualitative data”?
items.answer: Open question
items.markingKey: Open question: a question that lets respondents answer in their own words, producing qualitative data. [1]

items.stem: Explain what is wrong with this survey question and rewrite it: “Should our weak and useless leaders finally do something about lowering the voting age to 16?”
items.answer: Loaded wording: emotive words push respondents towards one answer. Improved, e.g.: “To what extent do you agree or disagree that the voting age should be lowered to 16? (Strongly agree / Agree / Neither / Disagree / Strongly disagree)”.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies fault; 1 mark explains effect on data; 1 mark neutral, single, clear rewrite [3]

items.stem: Ana is researching “How far do the benefits outweigh the drawbacks of the proposal that the United Nations member states should extend refugee protection to people displaced by climate change?”. The plan is to hand out a questionnaire to friends in the school canteen, including the question “Do you think migration caused by climate change is serious and that the United Nations member states should extend refugee protection to people displaced by climate change?”, and to interview one local politician. Explain the problem with the survey question.
items.answer: Double-barrelled question: it asks two things at once, so one answer cannot be interpreted.
items.markingKey: 1 mark fault; 1 mark effect on data [2]

items.stem: “Interviews are more useful than questionnaires for researching perspectives on threats to press freedom.” To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: For: Interviews reveal reasons and values behind a perspective. Follow-up questions clarify meaning. Against: Questionnaires reach larger, more representative samples. Closed questions produce data that can be compared and analysed statistically. Judgement: The best choice depends on the question; many reports combine both (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.stem: What is meant by “validity” in Global Perspectives?
options: Whether a method actually measures what it claims to measure.
Distortion caused when the sample does not represent the population.
The consistency of a method: whether it would give similar results if repeated.
How far findings from a sample can be applied to a wider population.
items.answer: Whether a method actually measures what it claims to measure.
items.markingKey: Validity: whether a method actually measures what it claims to measure. [1]

items.stem: A student uses a leaflet produced by a political party during an election campaign as evidence in a report on migration caused by climate change. Evaluate its credibility.
items.answer: Strength: it states the party’s position clearly. Weakness: its purpose is to win votes, so it is likely to be one-sided. It should be corroborated by independent evidence.
items.markingKey: 1 mark strength; 1 mark weakness; 1 mark corroboration or judgement [3]

items.stem: A survey of 625 randomly selected adults finds 58% support for the proposal that the parliament should ban live facial recognition in public places. The approximate 95% margin of error is given by 1/√n × 100 percentage points. What is the margin of error?
items.answer: ±4 percentage points

items.stem: A student researching the export of plastic waste to poorer countries surveyed 40 classmates (opportunity sample) using Likert-scale questions, and interviewed one official from an environmental NGO in Malaysia. The student concludes that “people in our country support the view that richer countries should be banned from exporting plastic waste”. Suggest how triangulation could strengthen the findings.
items.answer: Compare the survey with national polls and peer-reviewed studies, and interview stakeholders with different perspectives.
items.markingKey: 1 mark method; 1 mark how it checks findings [2]

items.stem: A survey of 900 randomly selected adults finds 58% support for the proposal that the riverside governments should negotiate a basin-wide water-sharing treaty. The approximate 95% margin of error is given by 1/√n × 100 percentage points. Calculate the margin of error and the likely range of true support. Can the researcher conclude that a majority supports the proposal?
items.answer: 1/√900 × 100 = ±3.3 points; range 54.7% to 61.3%. The whole range is above 50%, so a majority is likely.
items.markingKey: 1 mark margin; 1 mark range; 1 mark correct conclusion [3]

items.stem: “Student primary research adds little of value to a report on migration caused by climate change compared with published research.” To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: For: Student samples are small and unrepresentative. Published research uses larger samples and peer-reviewed methods. Against: Primary research can explore a local context or perspective that published research ignores. Triangulating local data with published studies can reveal differences. Judgement: Primary research is most valuable when clearly limited in its claims and used alongside published evidence.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–3 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (4–6 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (7–9 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [9]

items.stem: A report on the under-representation of women in parliaments includes evidence from a party official (prefers selection “on merit”) and from UN Women (supports temporary special measures such as quotas). Explain how the student could synthesise these perspectives rather than simply describe them.
items.answer: Identify where they agree and disagree, explain why (e.g. he believes quotas restrict local members’ choice; it works for gender equality under SDG 5), weigh the quality of the evidence each uses, and combine insights into a judgement on the question.
items.markingKey: 1 mark agreement/disagreement; 1 mark explains differences; 1 mark weighs evidence; 1 mark combined judgement [4]

items.stem: A report on low voter turnout among young people includes evidence from a libertarian think tank (opposes compulsory voting) and from a youth campaign group (supports automatic registration and voting at 16). Explain how the student could synthesise these perspectives rather than simply describe them.
items.answer: Identify where they agree and disagree, explain why (e.g. it believes not voting is a legitimate choice and the state should not coerce citizens; it wants young people’s interests represented), weigh the quality of the evidence each uses, and combine insights into a judgement on the question.
items.markingKey: 1 mark agreement/disagreement; 1 mark explains differences; 1 mark weighs evidence; 1 mark combined judgement [4]

items.stem: Respondents rated the statement “Governments should ban live facial recognition in public places” on a 1–5 scale. Responses: 1 Strongly disagree: 14; 2 Disagree: 5; 3 Neutral: 4; 4 Agree: 19; 5 Strongly agree: 15. What is the modal response?
items.answer: 4 Agree
items.markingKey: Most frequent = 4 Agree (19). [1]

items.stem: A student researching “How far do the benefits outweigh the drawbacks of the proposal that the political parties should introduce voluntary party quotas or all-women shortlists?” has three kinds of evidence: a survey of 400 adults (69% support the proposal that the parliament should introduce legal candidate quotas requiring parties to field a minimum share of women); 8 interviews, mostly expressing the concern that critics argue quotas may be seen as undermining selection on merit; and a peer-reviewed study finding that legal requirements are needed to change who is selected. (a) Evaluate which evidence should carry most weight in the conclusion. (b) Write a sentence that synthesises the three kinds of evidence.
items.answer: (a) The peer-reviewed study for effects (method checked, larger scale); the survey for public opinion; interviews for reasons. Weight depends on what part of the question is being answered. (b) e.g. “Although 69% of adults surveyed supported the proposal, interviewees worried that critics argue quotas may be seen as undermining selection on merit; the study suggests that legal requirements are needed to change who is selected, so support may be justified if this concern is addressed.”
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark evaluates each; 1 mark matches evidence to sub-question; 1 mark judgement [3] (b) 1 mark uses all three; 1 mark shows relationship; 1 mark leads to judgement [3]
